mcqs.question: A table range-partitioned by an auto-incrementing order ID keeps sending nearly all writes to one shard. Why?
options: New order IDs are sequential, so they all fall at the current end of the range, which one shard owns
Range partitioning doesn't support write operations at all
The shard holding the smallest IDs always receives every write by default
Range partitioning requires all writes to go through a single coordinator node
mcqs.explanation: Sequential keys keep landing in the same range as they're created, and that range belongs to one shard — the classic range-partitioning hotspot. Range partitioning fully supports writes; the smallest-ID shard isn't special, and there's no mandatory single coordinator for writes in this scheme.

mcqs.question: After switching from range to hash-based partitioning, a query for "all users who signed up this week" becomes slower and hits every shard. Why?
options: Hash partitioning scatters keys evenly, so adjacent signup dates no longer land on the same or nearby shards
Hash partitioning stores less data per shard than range partitioning
Hash functions cannot process date values
The query itself became invalid syntax under hash partitioning
mcqs.explanation: Hashing deliberately destroys key adjacency to spread writes evenly, which is exactly why range-style queries like "this week's signups" now have to scatter-gather across every shard. Hash partitioning handles dates fine as input; the query is still valid, just costlier.

mcqs.question: An orders table is sharded by `order_date` instead of `customer_id`. What's the main consequence for "get this customer's order history"?
options: The query becomes faster because dates are naturally sorted
It has no effect — shard key choice only affects write performance, not reads
It becomes a scatter-gather across every shard, since a customer's orders are spread across whatever dates they ordered on
The query can no longer be expressed at all
mcqs.explanation: Sharding by date groups orders by when they happened, not by who placed them, so a customer's history is scattered across every shard they've ever ordered from — forcing a scatter-gather. The query is still expressible, just expensive, and shard key choice clearly affects read cost, not only writes.

mcqs.question: A team shards a write-heavy event table by raw date to keep the design simple. What's the risk, and the better alternative?
options: There's no risk — date is a natural, sortable key
The system will run out of shards entirely once dates repeat each year
Switch every query to full table scans to avoid the sharding decision
Combine date with a high-cardinality field like a hashed user ID prefix, so writes spread while range queries still narrow the search
mcqs.explanation: Raw-date sharding concentrates all current writes on one "today" shard — a textbook hot shard. Combining date with a high-cardinality field spreads writes across shards while keeping range-style queries mostly narrowed. Dates don't repeat as a sharding collision issue, and full table scans defeat the point of sharding altogether.
